event: I have had a headache for two days.
rawInterpretation: There must be something seriously wrong with me.
alternateRealityChecks: Headaches can occur for many common reasons including stress, dehydration, poor sleep, or illness.
A symptom alone does not indicate a serious condition.
Many possible explanations are less severe than the worst-case scenario.
It is important to monitor symptoms rather than immediately assuming the most serious cause.
revisedInterpretation: The headache deserves attention, but I do not have enough evidence to conclude that it is serious.
chosenBehaviour: Monitor symptoms and seek medical advice if they persist or worsen.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The headache resolved after improving sleep and hydration.

event: I noticed a small unfamiliar pain in my chest.
rawInterpretation: I might be having a heart problem.
alternateRealityChecks: Chest discomfort can have many causes including muscle strain and stress.
One symptom does not provide enough information for a diagnosis.
Serious explanations are only one possibility among many.
Seeking professional evaluation is more useful than guessing.
revisedInterpretation: The symptom should be taken seriously, but I cannot determine the cause myself.
chosenBehaviour: Monitor symptoms and consult a healthcare professional if appropriate.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The discomfort was attributed to muscle strain.

event: I feel tired more often than usual.
rawInterpretation: I must have a serious illness.
alternateRealityChecks: Fatigue can have many causes including sleep, stress, workload, and lifestyle factors.
One symptom rarely provides enough information to identify a cause.
Many explanations are relatively common and manageable.
A professional assessment is more reliable than speculation.
revisedInterpretation: There are many possible explanations for the fatigue and more information is needed.
chosenBehaviour: Review sleep, stress, and lifestyle habits while monitoring symptoms.

event: I found health-related information online that matches some of my symptoms.
alternateRealityChecks: Many conditions share similar symptoms.
Online information is not a medical diagnosis.
It is easy to focus on information that confirms fears.
Professional evaluation is required to determine the actual cause.
revisedInterpretation: The information is interesting but does not confirm a diagnosis.
chosenBehaviour: Avoid self-diagnosis and seek professional guidance if needed.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The symptoms were linked to a common, non-serious issue.

rawInterpretation: The doctor must believe something is seriously wrong.
alternateRealityChecks: Additional tests are often used to gather information and rule out possibilities.
Doctors frequently order tests when symptoms are unclear.
The recommendation does not reveal the doctor's conclusions.
Testing can be part of routine caution.
revisedInterpretation: The additional testing is intended to improve understanding, not necessarily confirm a serious problem.
chosenBehaviour: Complete the testing and wait for results.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The tests did not reveal any serious issues.

event: I missed several workouts this week.
alternateRealityChecks: Health is influenced by long-term habits rather than a single week.
Temporary interruptions are common.
Missing workouts does not erase previous progress.
Consistency matters more than perfection.
revisedInterpretation: Missing a few workouts is unlikely to have a major impact on my long-term health.

event: I gained a few kilograms over the past several months.
rawInterpretation: I have completely lost control of my health.
alternateRealityChecks: Weight naturally fluctuates over time.
Health involves many factors beyond a single measurement.
Small changes do not define overall wellbeing.
Long-term patterns are more important than isolated changes.
revisedInterpretation: The weight gain may indicate changes worth understanding, but it does not define my overall health.
chosenBehaviour: Review habits objectively rather than reacting emotionally.
outcomeOneWeekLater: A practical health plan was created.

event: A family member was diagnosed with a health condition that runs in families.
rawInterpretation: I will probably develop the same condition.
alternateRealityChecks: Family history can influence risk but does not determine outcomes.
Many factors contribute to health conditions.
Risk is not the same as certainty.
Preventive care and healthy habits can be beneficial.
revisedInterpretation: I may have some increased risk, but that does not mean the condition is inevitable.
chosenBehaviour: Discuss family history with a healthcare professional.

event: I occasionally struggle to fall asleep.
alternateRealityChecks: Temporary sleep difficulties are common.
Sleep quality often fluctuates due to stress and life circumstances.
One difficult period does not predict the future.
Sleep habits can often be improved.
revisedInterpretation: The sleep difficulties are frustrating but not necessarily permanent.

event: I got out of breath while exercising.
rawInterpretation: There must be something seriously wrong with me.
alternateRealityChecks: Breathlessness during exercise can have many explanations.
Fitness level, intensity, and environment all play a role.
One observation does not provide enough information for conclusions.
Further observation may provide useful context.
revisedInterpretation: The experience may be related to several factors and should be evaluated in context.
chosenBehaviour: Pay attention to patterns and consult a professional if concerns continue.

event: Several members of my family have developed diabetes.
rawInterpretation: I am destined to develop diabetes too.
alternateRealityChecks: Family history influences risk but does not determine outcomes.
Lifestyle, environment, and preventive care also play important roles.
Risk and certainty are not the same thing.
Medical guidance can help manage known risks.
revisedInterpretation: My risk may be higher, but the future is not predetermined.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on healthy habits and regular check-ups.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I developed a clearer understanding of preventive actions.

event: My test results showed one value slightly outside the normal range.
rawInterpretation: This proves that I have a serious disease.
alternateRealityChecks: Test results need to be interpreted in context.
Minor deviations can occur for many reasons.
One result does not automatically indicate a major problem.
Professional interpretation is necessary.
revisedInterpretation: The result deserves attention, but it does not support a definite conclusion on its own.
chosenBehaviour: Review the results with my healthcare provider.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The variation was not considered clinically significant.

rawInterpretation: I must be developing a serious memory problem.
alternateRealityChecks: Minor forgetfulness is common, particularly during busy or stressful periods.
One symptom alone is not enough to draw conclusions.
Stress, fatigue, and attention can affect memory.
Professional evaluation is more reliable than self-diagnosis.
revisedInterpretation: The forgetfulness may have many ordinary explanations.
chosenBehaviour: Monitor patterns rather than assuming the worst.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Improved rest appeared to help concentration.

event: I have experienced increasing stress and occasional stomach discomfort for several months.
rawInterpretation: I probably have a serious illness.
alternateRealityChecks: The symptoms deserve attention because they have persisted.
Stress can affect physical health in meaningful ways.
Many possible explanations remain open.
The evidence supports seeking evaluation rather than assuming a diagnosis.
revisedInterpretation: The symptoms are worth discussing with a healthcare professional, but I do not know the cause.
chosenBehaviour: Schedule a medical appointment and track symptoms.
outcomeOneWeekLater: A plan was established to investigate and address possible causes.

event: A doctor told me that some lifestyle changes would improve my health.
rawInterpretation: I have already damaged my health beyond repair.
alternateRealityChecks: Lifestyle recommendations are often intended to improve future outcomes.
Health usually exists on a spectrum rather than being permanently damaged or perfectly healthy.
Positive changes can have meaningful benefits.
The recommendation suggests improvement is possible.
revisedInterpretation: There are areas I can improve, and positive changes may still have a meaningful impact.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on gradual and sustainable improvements.
